title: My day
topic: reflexive verbs in the present; telling the time
why: First lesson of the "My everyday life" unit: you reuse the regular present to describe your day with reflexive verbs. You also learn to tell the time and discover the Spanish meal schedule, essential for living in Spain.

Me levanto: reflexive verbs

To describe your daily routine, Spanish uses lots of reflexive verbs. Where English says \"I get up\", Spanish says \"I raise myself\": me levanto. A small pronoun goes before the verb, then the verb is conjugated as you already know (levantar is a regular -ar verb).

levantarse (to get up)ducharse (to shower)
yome levantome ducho
túte levantaste duchas
él, ella, ustedse levantase ducha
nosotros, nosotrasnos levantamosnos duchamos
vosotros, vosotrasos levantáisos ducháis
ellos, ellas, ustedesse levantanse duchan

English has no pronoun at all in \"I get up\" or \"I shower\", so the trap is forgetting it. Remember:

  • \"we get up\" is nos levantamos: the pronoun is required, the subject isn't;
  • \"you all get up\" (vosotros) is os levantáis: the pronoun is os;
  • se is used for he, she, usted and for they, ustedes: se levanta, se levantan;
  • in the infinitive, the pronoun is attached to the end: levantar → levantarse (to get up).

You already know one: me llamo, te llamas, se llama. It's the verb llamarse, conjugated exactly like levantarse.

Three verbs to learn as they are

These verbs change their vowel in the present; you'll see why later. For now, just remember the yo form:

InfinitiveMeaningI…
despertarseto wake upme despierto
vestirseto get dressedme visto
acostarseto go to bedme acuesto
Me despierto a las siete, me ducho y me visto.I wake up at seven, I shower and I get dressed.

The negation no goes before the pronoun: No me levanto temprano (I don't get up early). And where English says \"my teeth\", Spanish uses the article: me lavo los dientes (I brush my teeth).

¿Qué hora es? Telling the time

First, the numbers you need for the time:

NumberSpanishNumberSpanish
1uno7siete
2dos8ocho
3tres9nueve
4cuatro10diez
5cinco11once
6seis12doce

For minutes, add veinte (20) and veinticinco (25).

Es la una, son las dos

You don't say a word for \"o'clock\": just the feminine article and the number (the hidden word is la hora, \"the hour\").

TimeSpanish
1:00Es la una.
2:00Son las dos.
3:05Son las tres y cinco.
4:15Son las cuatro y cuarto.
5:30Son las cinco y media.
6:40Son las siete menos veinte.
7:45Son las ocho menos cuarto.
9:00 sharpSon las nueve en punto.
  • Es la una in the singular; for all other hours, son las… in the plural.
  • After half past, start from the next hour and take away the minutes with menos, like \"a quarter to eight\" or \"twenty to seven\".
  • For \"at eight\", say a las ocho (and a la una). The question is ¿A qué hora…? (At what time…?)

The time of day

  • With a time (like a.m. / p.m.): de la mañana (in the morning), de la tarde (in the afternoon), de la noche (at night, in the evening): a las diez de la noche.
  • Without a time: por la mañana (in the morning), por la tarde (in the afternoon), por la noche (in the evening, at night): Me ducho por la mañana.
  • 12 noon = las doce or el mediodía; midnight = las doce de la noche or la medianoche.

Greetings depend on the time: Buenos días (good morning), Buenas tardes (good afternoon, until nightfall), Buenas noches (good evening, and also good night).

", "

Meals and the Spanish schedule

You already know the meal verbs: desayunar, comer, cenar. What surprises visitors is the time: in Spain, people eat late!

The mealThe verbThe usual time
el desayunodesayunar7–9 a.m.
la comidacomer2–3:30 p.m.
la meriendamerendararound 6 p.m.
la cenacenar9–10:30 p.m.

Careful: comer means \"to eat\" in general, but also \"to have lunch\", the midday meal. And la comida means that midday meal (or food in general).

—¿A qué hora comes? —Como a las dos y media.—What time do you have lunch? —I have lunch at half past two.
En España, la gente cena a las diez de la noche.In Spain, people have dinner at ten at night.

Notice la gente (people): it's a feminine singular noun, so the verb is singular, unlike English \"people are\": la gente cena, la gente come.

Describing your morning

Me despierto a las siete menos cuarto. Me levanto a las siete, me ducho y me visto. Desayuno a las siete y media.I wake up at a quarter to seven. I get up at seven, I shower and I get dressed. I have breakfast at half past seven.
Por la noche ceno a las diez y me acuesto a las doce.In the evening I have dinner at ten and I go to bed at midnight.

La merienda is the afternoon snack, for children and adults alike. Merendar also changes its vowel (meriendo): mostly just remember the noun la merienda.
